cards.text: Friend, look at this guest list: Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, his whole army, every kingdom under his control and ALL the other nations, fighting against Jerusalem and its surrounding cities. I can't get that many helpers for one batch of cookies. In the middle of all that, the word of the LORD comes to Jeremiah the prophet.

cards.question: With Jerusalem under attack, who does the LORD send Jeremiah to speak to?

cards.text: The message for King Zedekiah opens hard. The LORD says He's about to hand this city over to the king of Babylon.

cards.question: Once the king of Babylon has Jerusalem in his hand, what does the LORD say he'll do to it?
The LORD tells Zedekiah that he himself will escape the king of Babylon's grasp.

cards.text: Zedekiah won't just get caught. He'll see the king of Babylon eye to eye and speak with him face to face, and friend, that is the one meeting NOBODY wants on their calendar.

cards.question: After Zedekiah is captured and meets the king of Babylon, where does the LORD say Zedekiah will go?

cards.text: Then the message turns. "Yet hear the word of the LORD, O Zedekiah king of Judah."

cards.question: The LORD tells Zedekiah he will not die by the ___. He will die in ___.
When Zedekiah dies, what will people do for him, just like they did for the kings before him?

answers.text: Burn spices and lament for him
Carve his name on a great tomb

cards.text: People will cry out for him, "Alas, O master!" And the LORD seals it: "For I Myself have spoken this word, declares the LORD."
So Jeremiah delivers every one of those words to Zedekiah, right there in Jerusalem. Meanwhile, the king of Babylon's army keeps fighting against Jerusalem and the remaining cities of Judah.

cards.question: While Babylon's army fights against Jerusalem, Judah still has plenty of fortified cities standing.

cards.text: Lachish and Azekah. That's the whole list of fortified cities Judah has left. When your list of strongholds fits on a sticky note, friend, that's not a list. That's a cry for help.
Now the word comes to Jeremiah about something King Zedekiah did. He made a covenant with all the people in Jerusalem to proclaim liberty.

cards.question: Under Zedekiah's covenant, only the male Hebrew slaves were to go free.

cards.text: The officials and all the people agree, and friend, they actually DO it. They obey and release them.

cards.question: The Hebrew slaves in Jerusalem have been set free. How long does their freedom last?

answers.text: Until the people change their minds
For the rest of their lives

cards.text: They take back the servants they freed and force them to be slaves again. That's not a change of heart, friend. That's a U-turn with the blinker off.
So the word of the LORD comes to Jeremiah. The LORD reminds them of the covenant He made with their forefathers when He brought them out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.

cards.question: In that covenant from the days of Egypt, when did a Hebrew servant have to be set free?
The forefathers listened to the LORD and kept that law about freeing Hebrew servants.

cards.text: But the LORD says this generation started out right. They recently repented and did what pleased Him, each one proclaiming freedom for his neighbor.

cards.question: Where did the people make their covenant before the LORD to free their neighbors?

answers.text: In the house that bears His Name
In the courtyard of the guard
At the gate of the city

cards.text: Then they changed their minds. Each one took back the servants he had set at liberty to go wherever they wanted.

cards.question: By taking back the servants they had freed, the people have ___ the LORD's name.

cards.text: Watch this, friend. They wouldn't proclaim freedom for a brother or a neighbor, so the LORD takes that same word, freedom, and turns it around.

cards.question: The people wouldn't proclaim freedom for their brothers. So what kind of freedom does the LORD proclaim for them?

answers.text: Freedom to fall by sword and plague and famine
Freedom to leave the city in peace
Freedom to choose a new king

cards.text: There it is: "freedom to fall by sword, by plague, and by famine!" And the LORD says He'll make them a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth.
They made that covenant by cutting a calf in two and passing between its pieces. Friend, when you walk between the pieces, you are NOT signing in pencil.

cards.question: The LORD says He'll treat those who broke the covenant like what?

answers.text: The calf they cut in two
The ram caught in the thicket
The goat sent into the wilderness

cards.question: Only the priests passed between the pieces of the calf.

cards.text: The officials of Judah and Jerusalem, the court officials, the priests and all the people of the land. Everybody who walked between those pieces is in this.

cards.question: The LORD says He'll shield the people who passed between the pieces from their enemies.

cards.text: "Their corpses will become food for the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth." And Zedekiah and his officials go into the hands of Babylon's army, the same army that had withdrawn from them.

cards.question: The king of Babylon's army had pulled back from Jerusalem. What does the LORD say He'll do about that army?

answers.text: Bring them back to this city

cards.text: "They will fight against it, capture it, and burn it down." Burn it down. Same words the LORD gave Zedekiah at the very start.

cards.question: The LORD says He will make the cities of Judah a ___ without inhabitant.

findings.problem: The joke mixes two images. It calls the attacking army a "guest list," which blends the comparison into the Bible setting. Then it compares that army to getting helpers for a batch of cookies. The core action is armies coming against a city to fight, but the comparison is about gathering help, so the actions don't match.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: The joke breaks the one-image rule. "Guest list" is laid directly onto the Bible scene of nations fighting Jerusalem, and then a second cookie-helper image is added on top.

rule.text: One image only. Never blend the comparison with the Bible setting.

findings.problem: Blank 1 asks the baker to guess the exact wording "sword" from sword, plague and fire. They are all ways to die, and nothing on the earlier cards lets the baker reason which one the text uses. Plague even shows up later in the passage (34:17) as a judgment. Only blank 2 ("peace") can be reasoned out from "the message turns."

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The wrong answer "Until the seventh year comes" puts the "seventh year" in front of the baker. Card 7 then asks when a Hebrew servant had to be freed, and its right answer is "Every seventh year," so this card gives that answer away.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: The wrong answer "Every fiftieth year" can be argued as right. The Jubilee law from the same Sinai covenant also frees Hebrew servants (Leviticus 25:39-41), and the question asks about the covenant made when God brought them out of Egypt.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: Both wrong answers ("honored" and "glorified") are positive words. Neither is believable for people who took back the servants they had freed. They also mean nearly the same thing as each other, so "profaned" stands out as the only possible answer.

rule.text: For why and meaning questions, wrong answers only need to be believable.

findings.problem: Story card 4 tells the baker that they cut "a calf in two." The right answer here is "The calf they cut in two," nearly word for word. The ram and the goat never appear in the passage, so the setup leaves only one possible pick.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The wrong answers "refuge" and "fortress" aren't believable. The question says the cities will be "without inhabitant," and they come right after a run of judgments. Only "desolation" fits, so the right answer stands out instead of being reasoned out.

rule.text: For why and meaning questions, wrong answers only need to be believable.
